title: The blessing refrain
hookLine: a scholarship, a clean scan, a win: an old discourse's highest blessings start smaller
tomorrow: why do the discourses start with someone else's ears?

lines: A SCHOLARSHIP, A CLEAN SCAN, A WIN.
cards: Ask a room what a blessing looks like and the answers come big: a scholarship, a clean scan, a new baby, a championship. Fair enough. Those are blessings.
An old Buddhist discourse asks the same question, and its answer starts much smaller, small enough to fit on a Tuesday. It comes with a refrain you can say after almost anything done well.

teach.b: The Mangala Sutta opens at night. A deity, lighting up the whole grove, comes to the Buddha and says that gods and humans have pondered blessings: so what is the highest?
The answer comes in short verses, and every one ends the same way: etam mangalam uttamam. Etam, this. Mangala, a blessing.
Uttamam, highest. This is the highest blessing. And look at what's on the list.
Not keeping company with fools; keeping company with the wise.

teach.h: A CRAFT WELL LEARNED, PARENTS CARED FOR.
teach.b: Much learning, and a craft well learned. Words well spoken. Supporting mother and father.
Giving. Patience. Ordinary things, done well.
Now hang that refrain on this week. The heart in Pali: stop the harm, take up the good, clear your own mind. Come and see.
Thus indeed is he. Practicing well. Words you know now.
Skilled in good. Six lines from a week, each one small enough to live on a Tuesday.

how: The Mangala Sutta is one of the Theravada protection chants; monks chant it at blessings, house-warmings and weddings, and lay Buddhists chant along or listen with joined palms.

o: the chorus sung at the close of a temple festival
the line closing each verse: this is the highest blessing
a blessing monks say over the food before a meal

games.q: this week's lines — tap the pairs.
p: to be done by one skilled in good

s: mangala in this sutta means a lucky omen
the sutta's blessings are ways of living: wise company, learning, a craft, care for parents, giving, patience.
a craft well learned is on the list of highest blessings
much learning, and a craft well learned, sit beside words well spoken.

games.q: a friend rolls her eyes at anything religious but likes honest people. which of this week's lines would you hand her first?
o: iti pi so: thus indeed is he, the Buddha's qualities.
ehipassiko: come and see, check it for yourself.
games.why: the dhamma verse praises the teaching as come-and-see, known by the wise each for themselves. it asks for a look, not belief.

practice: Before the sit, do one small good thing within reach: refill a glass for someone, straighten what's crooked, put one thing back where it lives. Then sit, and say softly: etam mangalam uttamam.
Let the week's six lines come back one at a time, and rest between them.

wordCard.voice: The blessing refrain: etam mangalam uttamam, this is the highest blessing. It closes every verse of the Mangala Sutta.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: etam, this; mangalam, blessing; uttamam, highest.

carryVoice: Pocket this: the highest blessing, said after something small done well. A week of Pali, gathered.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 2.4 (Mangala Sutta): a deity lighting up Jeta's Grove asks about blessings; each verse ends etam mangalam uttamam (non-association with fools, association with the wise, much learning and a craft, well-spoken words, supporting mother and father, giving, patience …)
